# Nanonets gets Accel’s backing to improve AI-based workflow automation

[Jagmeet Singh](https://techcrunch.com/author/jagmeet-singh/)

5:01 AM PDT · March 12, 2024

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Ftechcrunch.com%2F2024%2F03%2F12%2Fnanonets-funding-accel-india%2F)[Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftechcrunch.com%2F2024%2F03%2F12%2Fnanonets-funding-accel-india%2F&text=Nanonets+gets+Accel%E2%80%99s+backing+to+improve+AI-based+workflow+automation&via=techcrunch)[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftechcrunch.com%2F2024%2F03%2F12%2Fnanonets-funding-accel-india%2F&title=Nanonets+gets+Accel%E2%80%99s+backing+to+improve+AI-based+workflow+automation&summary=Nanonets%2C+a+startup+using+AI+to+automate+back-office+processes%2C+has+raised+%2429+million+in+a+new+funding+round+led+by+Accel+as+it+seeks+to+improve+the+accuracy+of+automation+processes+that+involve+large+amounts+of+unstructured+data.+Processing+unstructured+data+from+documents+like+invoices%2C+receipts+and+purchase+orders+often+involves+repetitive+tasks+and+a+%5B%E2%80%A6%5D&mini=1&source=TechCrunch)[Share on Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftechcrunch.com%2F2024%2F03%2F12%2Fnanonets-funding-accel-india%2F&title=Nanonets+gets+Accel%E2%80%99s+backing+to+improve+AI-based+workflow+automation)[Share over Email](mailto:?subject=Nanonets+gets+Accel%E2%80%99s+backing+to+improve+AI-based+workflow+automation&body=Article%3A+https%3A%2F%2Ftechcrunch.com%2F2024%2F03%2F12%2Fnanonets-funding-accel-india%2F)[Copy Share Link](https://techcrunch.com/2024/03/12/nanonets-funding-accel-india/)

Nanonets, a startup using AI to automate back-office processes, has raised $29 million in a new funding round led by Accel as it seeks to improve the accuracy of automation processes that involve large amounts of unstructured data.

Processing unstructured data from documents like invoices, receipts and purchase orders often involves repetitive tasks and a lot of human resources. Nanonets, which primarily targets the financial services sector, says its AI platform aims to improve the efficiency of these processes and make them cost-effective.

A Y Combinator alum, the startup has built an AI platform through which it offers no-code solutions that, according to the company, can help businesses extract information from documents, emails, tickets, databases and the like, and convert them into actionable insights. The company’s AI platform uses machine learning architectures to analyze unstructured data from uploaded documents and extract useful information. Its no-code AI agents can be plugged into ERP platforms like QuickBooks, Xero, Sage and NetSuite to automate accounts payable processes, optimize supply chains by taking historical data from Square and Tableau, and summarize health reports from patient management systems.

[Nanonets](https://nanonets.com/) claims that while an invoice typically takes 15 minutes to process manually, its automated finance solutions can reduce the time taken to less than a minute. These solutions can work for processes like accounts payable, reconciliation, accounts receivable and expense management.

The startup intends to use the fresh funding for R&D to improve the accuracy of its system and invest in sales and marketing. It has about 100 employees, which includes most of its engineering team that’s based in India. The company also will use the new funding to increase its headcount.

The all-equity Series B round saw participation from Nanonets’ existing investors Elevation Capital and Y Combinator. It brings the startup’s total funding raised to $42 million, including its $10 million Series A round in 2022.

Prathamesh Juvatkar, co-founder and CTO at Nanonets, told TechCrunch that the startup initially used [convolutional neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network) (neural network architectures used in computer vision for image classification and object recognition) to examine images and detect featured objects. The startup later considered deploying graph neural networks, but eventually moved to transformers and embraced multimodal architectures after it saw that they were more accurate than existing machine learning technologies.

“Right now, in the back end, we have multiple architectures. Whenever we get a new customer, we train all of these models on the customer data and see which one gets better accuracy,” he said in an interview.

IIT Gandhinagar alumni Juvatkar and Sarthak Jain (CEO) co-founded Nanonets after selling Cubeit, a machine-learning platform that turned web pages into sharable mobile cards, to fashion portal Myntra in 2016.

Unlike many other AI startups that rely on large language models (LLMs) and GPTs, Nanonets prefers transformers to circumvent the issue of hallucinations, which occur when an AI system generates information that is not present in the given documents, but is generated based on the LLM’s knowledge.

Even though the machine learning architectures that Nanonets use are document-agnostic, the startup is targeting the financial services space because about 50%-55% of its customers are from that domain. It has offered a range of integrations to streamline finance operations. However, the company is gradually expanding to “more adjacent processes,” and has also started serving customers in healthcare and manufacturing, Juvatkar said.

Nanonets is not alone in the global market for AI-based workflow automation. The market is crowded with traditional optical character recognition (OCR) platforms as well as startups, such as Rossum AI and Hyperscience. Bigger companies like UiPath also offer workflow automation, but with structured data. Still, Juvatkar said Nanonets takes on the competition by offering a record 90% straight-through processing rate — the percentage of data processed without manual intervention.

“We win deals primarily because of accuracy, user experience and the quality of our integrations,” he said.

Nanonets offers its solutions in three different pricing tiers: Starter, Pro and Enterprise. Of these tiers, Juvatkar told TechCrunch, the Pro and Enterprise are the most significant contributors to the startup’s annual recurring revenue, with an equal split. The startup also offers tools to convert PDFs to Excel spreadsheets, CSV, JSON, XML and text, image to text and image to Excel. These converters have helped gain the attention of businesses that require automation and reach more than 34% of the global Fortune 500 companies over the last two years, the company said. Additionally, the startup has expanded its user base by four times over the previous 12 months, and currently has over 10,000 customers globally.

Nanonets has users across the world, but the U.S. accounts for about 40% of its revenues, followed by Europe, which contributes 30% to 35%, Juvatkar said.

Juvatkar told TechCrunch, without disclosing the numbers, that since the 2022 round, Nanonets’ revenue has consistently increased by three times per year. The startup aims to expand its top line by 2x to 3x this year, too.

Consistent revenue growth is one reason investors have been investing in AI startups despite the slowdown in global markets. Funding to AI startups soared to $21 billion in 2023 from $10 billion in 2022, while the number of deals dropped by 61 to 399 last year, per Tracxn. AI startups in the U.S. receive the most investments, followed by companies in China, U.K., Israel and India.

“We are thrilled to partner with Nanonets in their mission to revolutionize back-office operations with AI. Sarthak and his team have been dedicated to getting to the bottom of customer pain points and have built a powerful solution that fully automates business processes end-to-end. Nanonets stood out to us due to its comprehensive platform and its capability for Straight Through Processing (STP) — these qualities set Nanonets apart in the field of automation and have already demonstrated their positive impact to customers,” said Abhinav Chaturvedi, partner at Accel, in a prepared statement.

# PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

[Tim Fernholz](https://techcrunch.com/author/tim-fernholz/)

11:03 AM PST · November 10, 2026

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab [Physical Superintelligence (PSI)](https://psi.inc/), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve [an eighteen-year-old problem](https://psi.inc/research/aaronson-ambainis/) about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, [writes](https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10295) that he doesn’t quite understand the proof, but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and [explained](https://guyblanc.github.io/AA_Exposition.pdf) by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full \[Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture\] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound— “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”

Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the start-up Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world …nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before….and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”

“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

# OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google

[Lucas Ropek](https://techcrunch.com/author/lucas-ropek/)

10:49 AM PST · November 10, 2026

In an effort to make ChatGPT an even better consumer discovery engine, OpenAI is launching a host of new features designed to help companies control how users interact with their businesses.

On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the [kind of profiles](https://business.google.com/us/business-profile/) that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services. The feature is currently in beta.

Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.

“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”

In a move that calls to mind [Google’s Analytics](https://techcrunch.com/2021/05/13/google-analytics-prepares-for-life-after-cookies/), the Business Hub will also give users access to limited business insights. These insights will reveal how ChatGPT users interact with their products — including profile views, business mentions, website clicks, and other metrics.

Businesses will have to verify their profiles through a formal process, although the company did not share specifics of what that process would entail. Benji Shomair, VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”

![](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Screenshot-2026-11-10-at-9.25.01-AM.png?w=680)**Image Credits:** OpenAI

OpenAI previously tried to position ChatGPT as an e-commerce hub by which users could buy products directly. This effort — which used a commission fee system — was viewed as a potentially huge source of revenue and a way to make ChatGPT a more direct Amazon competitor. However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company [retired the effort](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/24/openais-plans-to-make-chatgpt-more-like-amazon-arent-going-so-well/), which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.

With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at. It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to make ChatGPT a direct e-commerce hub.
